blocks.text: In 1959 Rodney Porter used the enzyme papain to cut a rabbit IgG molecule into three pieces: two identical fragments that still bound antigen and one that did not. That experiment, and its logic, tells you almost everything about how an antibody is built and why different classes do different jobs.

blocks.markdown: An **antibody (immunoglobulin, Ig)** is a Y-shaped glycoprotein secreted by plasma cells (or displayed on B cells as the B cell receptor). The basic unit has **two identical heavy chains** and **two identical light chains**, held together by disulfide bonds and non-covalent forces. Light chains are of type κ or λ (one type per antibody). The heavy chain type defines the **class (isotype)**: μ (IgM), γ (IgG), α (IgA), ε (IgE), δ (IgD).

**Domains.** Each chain is folded into compact immunoglobulin domains of about 110 amino acids. The N-terminal domain of each heavy and light chain is the **variable region (Vₕ and Vₗ)**; the rest is the **constant region**. Within each variable region, three **hypervariable loops** (complementarity-determining regions, CDRs) come together to form the **antigen-binding site**. A basic antibody has two identical binding sites, so IgG is **bivalent**. A flexible **hinge region** lets the two arms move independently.

blocks.title: Fab and Fc
blocks.text: The Fab (fragment antigen-binding) contains the light chain and the Vₕ and Cₛ1 domains of the heavy chain; it carries the antigen-binding site. The Fc (fragment crystallisable) is formed by the remaining heavy-chain constant domains and carries the effector functions: binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes and mast cells, and to C1q to activate complement.

blocks.title: What would these fragments do?
blocks.prompt: IgG is digested with papain. Predict whether the fragments can (a) bind antigen, (b) agglutinate (cross-link) antigen particles, and (c) activate complement.

steps.text: Identify the fragments. Papain gives two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.
Antigen binding is a Fab function, so each Fab can bind antigen.
Agglutination needs two binding sites linked together. Each Fab has only one site, so it cannot cross-link particles; a F(ab')2 fragment (from pepsin) could.
Complement activation and Fc receptor binding are Fc functions, so neither Fab fragment can do them; the isolated Fc cannot bind antigen, so it does not act at the target.

blocks.answer: Fab fragments bind antigen but cannot agglutinate or activate complement; the Fc lacks antigen binding.

rows: Pentamer (with J chain) in serum; monomer as B cell receptor
First antibody made in a response; very effective at complement activation; agglutination; mainly intravascular
Most abundant in serum; opsonisation, complement activation, neutralisation, neonatal protection (crosses placenta); four subclasses
Monomer in serum; dimer (with J chain and secretory component) in secretions
Mucosal immunity (gut, airway, tears, saliva); breast milk; neutralisation without inflammation
Binds mast cells and basophils via FCεRI; defence against helminths; allergic disease
B cell receptor on naive B cells together with IgM; little secreted function
blocks.caption: The five classes

blocks.markdown: **Class switching.** A B cell first makes IgM and IgD with the same variable region. After T cell help, the heavy-chain constant region gene is changed by **class-switch recombination**: the DNA between the variable region and a downstream constant region gene is looped out, using the enzyme **activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)**. Cytokines from helper T cells (for example IL-4 for IgE, IFN-γ for IgG, TGF-β for IgA) direct which class is chosen. Importantly, the **variable region, and therefore antigen specificity, is unchanged**; only the effector function changes.

**Somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation.** In germinal centres, AID also introduces point mutations into the variable-region genes at a high rate (around 10^-3 per base pair per cell division, about a million times the background rate). Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but B cells whose mutations raise affinity for antigen are selected to survive. Over time the average **affinity** of antibodies for the antigen rises: **affinity maturation**.

blocks.caption: \mu = mutation rate per base pair per division, L = length of region in base pairs, d = number of divisions

blocks.title: How many mutations?
blocks.prompt: A B cell lineage in a germinal centre has an SHM rate of 1 × 10^-3 per base pair per division. The heavy-chain V region is 360 base pairs long. Estimate the average number of new mutations per cell per division, and after 10 divisions.

steps.text: Per division, multiply rate by length.
For 10 divisions, multiply by the number of divisions.
Interpret: roughly one in three cells gains a mutation per division, and on average several accumulate over ten divisions. Selection then enriches the beneficial ones.

blocks.answer: 0.36 mutations per division; about 3.6 after 10 divisions.

blocks.title: Two different changes
blocks.text: Class switching changes the constant region and therefore what the antibody does, but not what it binds. Somatic hypermutation changes the variable region and therefore how tightly it binds. Both depend on AID and on T cell help in the germinal centre.

points: Antibodies have two heavy and two light chains; the Fab (with Vₕ/Vₗ and CDRs) binds antigen, the Fc mediates effector functions.
IgM is the first and best complement fixer, IgG the most abundant and opsonising, IgA secretory at mucosae, IgE for mast cells and parasites, IgD is a B cell receptor.
Class switching changes class but not specificity; somatic hypermutation and selection raise affinity.

questions.stem: Which part of an immunoglobulin binds antigen?

options.text: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains
The constant region of the light chain

questions.correctOptionText: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains

distractorRationale.b: The hinge gives flexibility but does not bind antigen.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the CDRs of Vₕ and Vₗ form the binding site.
distractorRationale.d: Light chain constant domain does not form the binding site.

questions.explanation: The antigen-binding site is formed by the hypervariable loops (CDRs) of the heavy- and light-chain variable domains. The Fc, in contrast, is responsible for effector functions.

questions.stem: A researcher wants a fragment that can cross-link antigen particles but cannot activate complement or bind phagocyte Fc receptors. Which should she prepare?

distractorRationale.b: A single Fab is monovalent and cannot cross-link.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: F(ab')2 is bivalent and lacks the Fc.
distractorRationale.d: Intact IgM has Fc and activates complement.

questions.explanation: A bivalent fragment lacking the Fc is the F(ab')2 produced by pepsin. It can cross-link antigen but lacks Fc-mediated functions.

questions.stem: A newborn's gut is protected by antibody in breast milk. Which class is mainly responsible?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dimeric IgA with secretory component survives mucosal secretions and protects the gut surface.
distractorRationale.b: IgE binds mast cells and is not the main milk antibody.
distractorRationale.c: IgD is mostly a B cell receptor.
distractorRationale.d: Monomeric IgM is a B cell receptor; secreted IgM is pentameric.

questions.explanation: Breast milk contains secretory IgA, a dimer joined by a J chain and stabilised by secretory component, which resists degradation in the gut lumen and neutralises microbes at the mucosal surface.

questions.stem: Which class is the first to appear in a primary response and is the most efficient at activating complement?

distractorRationale.b: IgE is for mast cell-mediated responses.
distractorRationale.c: IgG activates complement but is not first and is less efficient per molecule than pentameric IgM.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: IgM is first, pentameric and potent at C1q binding.

questions.explanation: IgM is the earliest antibody secreted, and its pentameric structure with ten antigen-binding sites and multiple Fc regions makes it an excellent complement activator and agglutinator.

questions.stem: A B cell switches from IgM to IgG production. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The antibody now binds a different antigen
The variable region is unchanged, so the antigen specificity is preserved
The light chain type changes from κ to λ

questions.correctOptionText: The variable region is unchanged, so the antigen specificity is preserved

distractorRationale.a: Specificity does not change in class switching.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: only the heavy-chain constant region changes.
distractorRationale.c: Light chain type is fixed for a B cell after rearrangement.
distractorRationale.d: AID is required for the switch.

questions.explanation: Class switching replaces the heavy-chain constant region while retaining the rearranged variable region. Hence effector functions change but specificity does not.

questions.stem: Which statement about somatic hypermutation is correct?

options.text: It occurs mainly in the Fc constant region genes
It requires AID and increases average antibody affinity through selection
It produces random mutations that always increase affinity

questions.correctOptionText: It requires AID and increases average antibody affinity through selection

distractorRationale.b: Correct: AID introduces mutations; selection enriches high-affinity clones.
distractorRationale.c: T cell receptor genes do not undergo SHM.
distractorRationale.d: Most mutations are neutral or harmful.

questions.explanation: SHM targets V region genes in germinal centre B cells. Selection of B cells with higher affinity receptors by follicular dendritic cells and T follicular helper cells leads to affinity maturation.

questions.stem: Serum IgG concentration is 12 g/L. Assume the molar mass of IgG is 150,000 g/mol and that each molecule has two identical antigen-binding sites. Calculate the molar concentration of binding sites in µmol/L.
questions.explanation: IgG molar concentration = 12 / 150,000 = 8 × 10^-5 mol/L = 80 µmol/L. Each IgG has two binding sites, so the concentration of sites is 160 µmol/L.

questions.stem: In a germinal centre, a variable-region segment of 300 base pairs mutates at 1 × 10^-3 per base pair per cell division. What is the expected number of new mutations in the segment per cell per division?
questions.explanation: Expected mutations = 10^-3 × 300 = 0.3 per division. Over several divisions mutations accumulate, and B cells with beneficial mutations are selected.

questions.stem: Match IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE and IgD to their principal roles.
markingGuide: IgM: first response, pentameric, complement activation
IgG: most abundant, opsonisation, complement, placental transfer
IgA: secretory at mucosal surfaces, breast milk
IgE: mast cell binding, helminths and allergy
IgD: B cell receptor on naive B cells
questions.explanation: Each class has a distinct heavy chain and corresponding effector role.

questions.stem: Explain how class switching and somatic hypermutation each alter an antibody, and which structural region each acts on.
markingGuide: Class switching: constant region of the heavy chain; changes effector function, not specificity
Needs AID and T cell help/cytokines
SHM: variable-region genes; point mutations altering the binding site
Selection of higher-affinity clones gives affinity maturation
questions.explanation: The two processes are complementary: one adjusts function and the other fine-tunes binding.
